TOKYO, Nov 5 : Japan's biggest steelmaker Nippon Steel on Thursday raised its net profit forecast for fiscal 2026 by 52 per cent to 440 billion yen ($2.8 billion), citing stronger-than-expected earnings from its US Steel business. • The forecast, for the year ending March 2027, compares with the company's August estimate of 290 billion yen and a net profit of 17 billion yen in fiscal 2025 • Nippon Steel expects US Steel, including its Slovak subsidiary NSSK, to contribute 230 billion yen to full-year underlying business profit, up 50 billion yen from its previous forecast, helped by higher US steel prices • The company also expects stronger raw material prices to boost earnings in its raw-materials business. A one-off gain of 96 billion yen from an Arkansas state tax credit related to capital expenditure also contributed to the upgrade

He said strong steel prices were not only driven by tariffs but also by the strength of the US economy • For the April-September first-half, Nippon Steel booked a net profit of 263 billion yen, against a net loss of 113 billion yen a year earlier, despite the impact of the Middle East conflict, typhoons and heavy rains, mainly in Japan ($1 = 157.8400 yen)

FAST

SAN FRANCISCO, Nov 5 : Stunning victories by Democrats in US midterm elections this week have been interpreted by many as Americans repudiating tech industry plans to build data centers across the country. OpenAI has now embarked on new strategies to change their minds. The AI lab on Thursday laid out policies — in the works since August — intended to help the company build more trust with local communities and convince them that data centers will benefit them.  OpenAI said it will no longer use non-disclosure agreements with public officials when negotiating or discussing future sites, although proprietary information would still be under wraps. It will also give residents access to construction plans and their potential effect on traffic, noise and lighting.  OpenAI's chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane also said that these centers would be a source of ongoing jobs because the hardware within the data center would need to be updated every three to five years.

"These projects are not the types of data centers that people have historically thought about, which are some version of a black box in a pasture that did very little in terms of the economic utility for the communities they were in," he told reporters.  One OpenAI facility in southern Ohio is expected to create 2,500 long-term jobs with an average annual salary of $80,000, he said. Partners such as Oracle are building and own much of OpenAI's data center infrastructure, with the capacity dedicated to the startup. DATA CENTER OPPONENTS MAKE BIG GAINS In some of the biggest upsets of the elections, Democrats flipped governorships in Texas, Georgia and Ohio with candidates who have promised to pause new data center permits and tighten construction rules.  And of the 41 data center-related ballot measures voted on this week, all but one went against data centers, according to Ballotpedia.  Shares of data center operators and power companies that have been among the biggest beneficiaries of the AI building boom also tumbled on Wednesday as investors bet the Democratic sweep could bring tougher permitting, higher costs and a slower pace of construction.  "We need to do a better job of really communicating to people, to local communities, about why data centers can be beneficial to them," OpenAI President Greg Brockman said at a separate event on Wednesday.  OpenAI officials, along with many of their peers in tech, have spent the last two years trying to build ties with the administration of US President Donald Trump in hopes of shaping federal policy around AI.  OpenAI CEO Sam Altman donated $1 million to Trump's inaugural committee and later attended Trump's second inauguration. Last year, Brockman donated $25 million in his personal capacity to a Trump super PAC.  When asked about how the company would address skepticism from some Democrats, Lehane pointed to his extensive experience in the party. During the Clinton administration, he served as a top lawyer and spokesperson and he was also press secretary for Vice President Al Gore when he made his run for president.

Source: Reuters

FAST

NEW YORK, Nov 5 : US regulators contacted banks to check whether their systems had any vulnerabilities after last week's $6.3 billion hack of Binance, alert to the risks that a hack in crypto markets could affect traditional finance at a time that links have tightened.  Supervisors from the Federal Reserve and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency started reaching out to banks on Monday morning, asking about any unusual activity or disruption in their services, according to several sources familiar with the matter.  One source at a bank that regulators had contacted said there were no disruptions in its services. The source said bank employees prepared a list of talking points to discuss with customers, but they have since received few inquiries.    Banks have been studying the Binance hack, believed to be the largest financial heist in history, and are also doing diagnostics on their systems to ensure they are prepared to defend against a similar attack, according to two separate people familiar with the efforts.

Within hours of the attack, a cybersecurity team at one of the largest US banks reached out to counterparts at Binance, according to one of the sources. That team is working on an internal report that will lead to a review of the bank’s systems, and possibly cybersecurity updates. It was not yet clear whether the bank would be vulnerable to similar tactics used by the Binance hackers, according to the source.  Binance said it was unaware of conversations between bankers and regulators, and whether the hack had an impact on US banks. "We are in close contact with regulators all over the world, keeping them up to date on this security breach," a Binance spokesperson said. The Fed and OCC declined comment.  One of the people familiar with the matter said the big concern is that artificial intelligence models have been evolving quickly, making it a challenge for banks to keep up with hackers. He said banks are devoting a lot of resources to reviews and patches of cybersecurity codes. President Donald Trump has been a cheerleader for cryptocurrencies, and US bank regulators have smoothed the way for banks to get more active in crypto markets. For instance, the Federal Reserve revoked a 2022 rule that advised banks to get permission from regulators before launching any crypto-related activities.

Source: Reuters

FAST

LONDON, Nov 5 : Brent crude futures edged up on Thursday as investors weighed the future course of the US-Israeli war with Iran after President Donald Trump's Republican Party suffered heavy losses in midterm elections this week. Brent futures were up 78 cents, or 0.8 per cent, at $95.40 a barrel as of 0900 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures rose 11 cents, or 0.1 per cent, to $88.23. "The situation in the Middle East is still unresolved and that's why there is some modest recovery in prices at the moment," said Giovanni Staunovo, commodity analyst at UBS. Brent is more impacted by geopolitical factors, while WTI is a domestic US benchmark, Staunovo said.

Both tumbled by more than 8 per cent in the previous session to settle at their lowest since August 31. The conflict with Iran, which Trump launched alongside Israel in February, and the resulting higher fuel prices for US consumers were major grievances for voters in Tuesday's rout of Republicans. "Markets are assessing the impact of the midterm elections on Donald Trump's next steps with the Iran war, pricing in more likelihood for the war to end," said June Goh, senior oil analyst at Sparta Commodities. "However, there will be more volatility ahead as the path to full diplomacy to end the war is still wrought with many unknowns while the global strategic reserves have drawn very thin," she said. Uncertainty remains before the new Democratic-controlled Congress takes office in January, analysts said.  Citi said in a note there were concerns that with the midterms over, the White House could focus on its executive powers in foreign policy and potentially escalate conflict with Iran. Eurasia Group lowered its estimate for the chance of renewed US strikes on Iran to 60 per cent from 65 per cent, but also cut the probability of a deal to 10 per cent from 20 per cent, as Iran has held firm on its demands and Trump was unlikely to accept terms seen as a defeat. It raised the likelihood of a continued standoff to 30 per cent from 15 per cent. Despite the recent drop in oil prices, escalation is likely to produce a sharper increase into a band of $110 to $125 per barrel for Brent, Eurasia Group said in a note. Meanwhile, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said on Thursday that two oil tankers and a tugboat had caught fire in separate incidents after attempting to use unauthorised routes through the Strait of Hormuz. Crude shipments through this key waterway for most Gulf oil supplies have recovered to close to pre-war levels, according to analysts, though at a higher cost.  The resumption of Gulf supply has pushed the global oil market back into surplus after months of disruption caused by the war, JPMorgan said in a note on Wednesday. JPMorgan estimates the market returned to a surplus of 1.1 million barrels per day in September, widening to 1.4 million bpd in October, nearly matching last year's average of 1.3 million bpd. Commercial oil inventories in major consuming countries are near their lowest in 15 years and Iran could emerge from the US election outcome with greater resolve, said Mukesh Sahdev, CEO of energy consultancy XAnalysts. US crude, gasoline and distillate inventories all fell last week as demand hit its highest in a year, the Energy Information Administration said on Wednesday.

Source: Reuters

BENGALURU/MUMBAI: India's cybersecurity agency named the hacking group behind a wave of AI-driven attacks on financial firms and identified its tools, at least two of them linked to China, adding India to a growing list of countries where such tools have been used against banks. The group, which the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) calls "Crafty Falcon," has breached non-bank lenders, fintech firms and cryptocurrency exchanges, according to an advisory issued on Wednesday (Nov 4). CERT-In did not say who was behind the breaches or where the organisation operates. The advisory came after a spate of cyberattacks on Indian banks and non-bank lenders in recent weeks, even as authorities issued warnings and the Reserve Bank of India tightened cybersecurity checks.

CERT-In said the attackers use publicly available AI tools to automate break-ins "at machine speed", calling the threat "active and ongoing". It named four tools: ARTEX, PentAGI, Cairn and CyberStrikeAI. Security researchers have linked at least two of them to China. China-made ARTEX has been used in attacks on South Korean banks since late September, cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike has said. It said a China-linked group also used the tool in an espionage campaign targeting more than 200 organisations in at least 14 countries. CERT-In did not name the affected companies or say how much money was stolen. The agency did not say the attacks were state-sponsored and the tools it named have been freely available online. ARTEX, however, was made private by its developer last month after it was linked to the South Korean attacks. CERT-In, the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre and India's IT ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Related:

Rogue AI agents broke into Indian firms' live systems, government says

South Korea's Lee says AI appears to have been used in bank hacks

PAYMENT INTERFACES TARGETED CERT-In said Crafty Falcon "surveys its targets with machine intelligence" and moves money by invoking victims' own payment and disbursement systems. Attacks were timed around holidays, weekends and other low-monitoring periods to delay detection. Firms that had fixed flaws after earlier alerts were attacked again after incomplete remediations were made, it said. Reuters previously reported, citing a police complaint, that last month two Mumbai-based non-bank lenders lost about US$2 million in more than 700 unauthorised instant transfers from accounts of India's third-largest lender ICICI Bank on Oct 8 and 9. The complaint said hackers compromised its application programming interfaces (APIs), the software links banks use to connect with non-bank lenders and fintech firms to send loan-disbursal instructions. State Bank of India , the country's largest lender, disclosed a dark-web leak of 3,897 customer records last month. Spandana Sphoorty Financial, a non-bank lender, reported unauthorised debits from a bank account on Nov 1, and AU Small Finance Bank said it was probing a potential customer-data leak. CERT-In did not say which incidents were linked to Crafty Falcon.

Source: Reuters/aj

TOKYO, Nov 5 : Sony on Thursday reported a 45 per cent rise in second-quarter operating profit, beating market estimates, while Nintendo reported an earnings slide that missed market expectations. The divergent fortunes of the two companies come as technology firms around the world grapple with a shortage of memory chips due to the AI boom, affecting a wide range of products including smartphones and computers. Sony's operating profit came in at 622.3 billion yen ($3.95 billion), better than an average estimate of 505 billion yen from 12 analysts polled by LSEG. Contributors to the stronger performance, which led the Japanese entertainment-and-technology conglomerate to increase its full-year profit outlook by 9 per cent, included the hit movie "Spider-Man: Brand New Day."

"Sony is the bigger winner today and their success could have been even bigger if more PlayStation 5 Pro units were available," said Serkan Toto, founder of the Kantan Games consultancy.   Sony, a major manufacturer of image sensors used in smartphones, also lifted its outlook for its chips and music divisions. Sony's games business is expected to be a major beneficiary of the launch of "Grand Theft Auto VI" on November 19, but is grappling with higher memory prices. Companies flagging the impact include iPhone maker Apple, which this week pointed to pressure on margins during the holiday quarter.  In July, the PlayStation maker said it had secured the amount of memory needed to meet its projected sales volume this year.  NINTENDO PROFIT SLIDES The memory crunch and a lack of high-profile titles for the Switch 2 have caused concern among Nintendo investors. The Kyoto-based company said operating profit declined 16 per cent to 73.9 billion yen in the quarter, below analyst estimates, and sales also fell. There has been no major change to the memory situation and Nintendo is in a position to secure sufficient quantities, President Shuntaro Furukawa said. The company, which unveiled a price increase earlier in the year, is not considering additional changes, Furukawa said. Nintendo maintained its full-year profit forecast and its outlook for sales of 16.5 million Switch 2 units. The company launched "The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time" on Thursday; the title received positive reviews. The "Zelda" game should sell well and give Nintendo a solid quarter, but the company will not release blockbuster titles until the next fiscal year, Toto of Kantan Games said. AI DISRUPTION FEARS Amid concerns about chip access, Sony sold 2.6 million PlayStation 5 units during the second quarter, down from 4 million a year earlier. Some observers expect Sony to launch a successor gaming device in late 2028. With memory prices a challenge, maintaining active user engagement will be key to supporting profitability as Sony invests in its new platform, Chief Financial Officer Lin Tao said. Shares of Sony, which the market has worried could be vulnerable to AI disruption, have been buoyant in recent weeks. Sony closed up 7 per cent ahead of its earnings report on Thursday.  ($1 = 157.8400 yen)

AMSTERDAM, Nov 5 : From hacked supermarket fridges and a record cryptocurrency theft at Binance to an emergency over flaws in widely used web software, companies worldwide are facing a wave of cyber threats executives say AI is accelerating and making more sophisticated. The surge is straining IT departments, with staff working overnight to patch software vulnerabilities, prompting some companies to turn to and increase investment in AI-powered security tools to help manage the workload. A cyberattack on European supermarkets on Monday, the second in three weeks in which hackers raised refrigerator and freezer temperatures, forcing retailers to discard millions of dollars' worth of spoiled food, underscored the urgency. "It's a never-ending game of cat and mouse, with very high stakes," said Marnie Wilking, chief security officer at travel platform Booking.com.

"We shut down one route, and before we've even finished rolling out the fix, the bad guys have moved on to the next," she said, adding that hundreds of engineers at the company were now building AI-powered defence systems. Nearly 37,000 security flaws in software or computer systems were reported in the third quarter of 2026, tripling from a year earlier, according to the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures list, an international registry of disclosed security flaws. "We're seeing events of a magnitude every week, or even every couple of days, that used to be months apart," Markus Noga, chief technology officer of German web hosting company Ionos, which serves seven million customers, told Reuters. Ionos said it changed its security practices after seeing a spike in vulnerabilities in July, deploying AI-based monitoring systems to scan for threats and using AI-assisted tools to install patches on its systems around the clock. "I'm kind of limited to what a nine-to-five office hours team can do and that's no longer good enough," Noga said. CYBER THREATS DRIVE DEFENSIVE SPENDING Binance, hit by hackers who stole $6.3 billion worth of cryptocurrency, said it would increase investment in AI-enhanced detection systems. The Port of Rotterdam is working on an AI-powered "cyber shield", while Siemens is testing advanced AI models for defensive security. Dutch-based grocer Ahold Delhaize, which operates the Stop & Shop and Giant Food chains in the US, was hit by two hacks in the past month. The first, in mid-October, led to more than €200 million ($225 million) in sales losses and prompted a profit warning. In that incident, Ahold took its websites and apps offline for a week after detecting an intrusion. This week, some of its stores in Belgium and Luxembourg were among those hit by cyberattacks on refrigerators across a dozen European countries. "We're adjusting to a new reality," CFO Jolanda Poots-Bijl told Reuters, adding smaller firms were particularly exposed. At the same time, AI is a defensive tool, she said. "AI also helps us to detect and to restore in a much faster way than we were ever able to do in the past," she added. McKinsey projects the global market for cybersecurity products and services sold by outside vendors will grow from $223 billion in 2025 to $346 billion by 2029. AI TOOLS HELP RESEARCHERS RECREATE HACKS The refrigerator cyberattacks show how AI is putting pressure on companies to patch systems quickly once a vulnerability is found, said Sean Tufts, field chief technology officer at cybersecurity firm Claroty. Claroty published research in August, months before the attacks began, outlining weaknesses in refrigeration controllers. After a first wave of attacks hit stores in France on October 11, Claroty researchers used widely available AI tools to reproduce the flaws and take control of a test device, highlighting the risk of further attacks. "We were able to recreate it for six dollars and 28 minutes," Tufts said. The October 21 disclosure of two AI-discovered flaws in the PHP programming language, which underpins many websites, prompted governments and companies from Tokyo to Helsinki to take websites offline as a precaution. US internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare reported that attempts to exploit PHP flaws rose from thousands to millions within hours of their disclosure. AI-discovered bugs could lead to more disruption in future, it told Reuters. "The threat is real, it's growing," said Kraft Heinz CEO Steve Cahillane, adding cybersecurity was "more important today than it was yesterday and will be even more important tomorrow". At Swiss building materials maker Holcim, which took its website offline around 9:30 p.m. (1930 GMT) on October 21 to install PHP fixes and restore service before midnight, Chief Financial Officer Steffen Kindler echoed those comments. "We need to get smarter. Both sides are heavily equipped," he said. "Both sides use AI, and that race is continuing." ($1 = 0.8905 euros)

Source: Reuters

Nov 5 : Microsoft will not exercise an option to more than double the size of its existing agreement with AI cloud provider Nscale to rent more computing power at a Texas data center, according to a person familiar with the matter. The Financial Times, which first reported the news on Thursday, said a potential deal extension would have been worth tens of billions of dollars for Nscale. The person, who declined to be named because the matter is confidential, said Microsoft's decision to not expand the contract was made several months ago, before Nscale filed for its IPO in September, and added that its existing Texas contract with Microsoft was not affected. The companies struck a deal last year for Nscale to deploy around 200,000 Nvidia AI chips under an expanded agreement with Microsoft across its data centers in Europe and the US.

JAKARTA: Indonesia's economy expanded 5.47 per cent in the third quarter from a year earlier, official data showed on Thursday (Nov 5), faster than the 5.18 per cent forecast in a Reuters poll. Indonesia's economic growth in the second quarter stood at 5.29 per cent. Southeast Asia's largest economy has contended with weaker investor sentiment this year amid heightened scrutiny of the government's fiscal plans and its broader policy directions, as well as lingering downgrade risks on its stock market . Growth was supported by sectors such as manufacturing, including the processing of palm oil to produce fuel as Indonesia expanded its mandatory biodiesel programme, the statistics bureau said. The 2026 state budget projects economic growth of 5.4 per cent, although finance minister Suahasil Nazara has said it could slightly exceed that target and reach 5.5 per cent this year. The target falls within Bank Indonesia's GDP growth outlook range of 4.9 per cent to 5.7 per cent. At its meeting last month, the central bank said the domestic economy remained resilient but required further strengthening. President Prabowo Subianto , who took office two years ago, aims to lift economic growth to 8 per cent by 2029.

Nov 5 : The euro rose for a fourth straight session on Thursday, supported by lower energy prices amid hopes that the risk of escalation in the Iran conflict could ease after Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections. A resolution of the conflict could restore Middle East oil flows disrupted by the war. However, uncertainty remained elevated with Citi saying concerns that the White House could escalate tensions with Iran persisted after the midterm vote. Democrats swept to majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives, spurring gains in US Treasuries and global equities, though doubts remained about whether the new Congress would be as accommodating to the AI sector.  The euro was up 0.16 per cent at $1.1268, after reaching $1.1273 on Wednesday, its highest level since October 6.

"On balance, we see political developments overnight as supportive of a continued bottoming out in the euro/dollar: lower energy and global policy risk premium but higher AI implementation risks should on balance weaken the dollar," said George Saravelos, global head of forex strategy at Deutsche Bank. While typically a fall in share prices boosts the safe-haven dollar, Saravelos has argued that an unprecedented US reliance on foreign equity flows has flipped the correlation, and a fall in tech stocks would now push the greenback down. Analysts said that the euro could nonetheless face renewed pressure as investors temper expectations for further European Central Bank monetary tightening while concerns linger over France's fiscal trajectory and ability to curb budget deficits. Hundreds of thousands of protesters are expected to march through French cities and public workers to strike on Thursday.  Rising public debt and the rapid expansion of non-bank finance could curb the ECB's ability to set the appropriate monetary policy, ECB board member Isabel Schnabel said on Thursday. The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies, fell 0.10 per cent to 101.38, after hitting 101.21 in the Asian session, the lowest since September 30. Despite the political shift in the US, expectations for the Federal Reserve's interest rate path remained largely intact. Markets are pricing in an 80.7 per cent chance of a rate increase of at least 25 basis points from the Fed at its December meeting, according to CME FedWatch, up from 77.4 per cent in the prior session.  Sterling strengthened 0.05 per cent to $1.3478, poised for its seventh straight daily rise, ahead of the Bank of England's policy announcement on Thursday. The yen gained after minutes from the Bank of Japan's September meeting, when policymakers raised rates to a 31-year high of 1.25 per cent, reinforced bets for further interest rate hikes. The BOJ minutes showed some board members signalling a chance of faster-paced increases. Markets now widely expect the BOJ's next hike to come in December. The yen rose 0.14 per cent to 158.18 per dollar.  In cryptocurrencies, bitcoin BTC=> gained 0.33 per cent to $80,403 and ether rose 0.28 per cent to $2,421.52.

Nov 5 : Australian data centre operator NEXTDC said on Thursday its board considered an aftermarket book build by an entity owned by Goodman Group and Digital Realty to be "opportunistic", and that it had received no takeover proposal. Shares of NEXTDC rallied in early trade, jumping as much as 45.8 per cent to A$9.52 by 2336 GMT and eyeing its strongest intraday gain ever. The stock had lost 45.8 per cent in October. On Wednesday, Goodman Group and Digital Realty offered to buy up to 9.9 per cent of NEXTDC in a deal worth about A$715 million ($501.14 million), Reuters reported, citing a term sheet. The share purchase comes after NEXTDC's stock plunged in October, when the company announced a power delay at its M3 Melbourne site, cut its guidance and shelved new development. The deal would give two rival data centre operators a stake of nearly 10 per cent in the Australian data centre operator.

NEXTDC said it noted the statement by Goodman and Digital Realty to investors during the aftermarket book build that they have "no intention of submitting a control proposal or making a takeover bid for the company at this time, but reserve their right to do so." "The share raid comes two weeks after NEXTDC's 21 October 2026 announcement of the M3 Melbourne power delay and revised FY27 guidance, and was made through an aftermarket book build open only to institutional investors," the firm added in its statement, saying that the board would consider any bona fide takeover approaches on their merits.  NEXTDC said in October it would also shelve all new development projects and land acquisitions for the foreseeable future. It also said it would evaluate capital recycling opportunities, including potential sales of selected development sites. Both Digital Realty and Goodman Group did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comments. ($1 = 1.4267 Australian dollars)

FAST

SYDNEY, Nov 5 : An inquiry into data centres by Australia's most populous state found approvals failed to consider the cumulative effect on resources and infrastructure but stopped short of calling for a moratorium, prompting a blistering rebuke from its chair. The report by the New South Wales cross-party inquiry reflects a growing tension facing lawmakers globally as they navigate an AI-led buildout that McKinsey estimates will be worth $7 trillion by 2030: they want to benefit from the boom but communities are putting up increasingly robust resistance. The tension is especially strong in New South Wales, of which Sydney is the capital, where developer NextDC and ChatGPT owner OpenAI are awaiting approval for a data centre. There is a state election next March, and already residents in one suburb prompted a smaller project to be withdrawn. The report found the state lacked a coherent strategy to manage the data centre boom's impact on water, electricity and infrastructure. It warned current guidelines may underestimate future power demand and water supply limits, and that "clustering" facilities could create infrastructure pressures.

"The current planning framework assesses data centres primarily as individual developments despite many impacts being cumulative in nature," it said. "Data centre ... impacts are cumulative and are being felt across communities and other industries." But it stopped short of recommending a halt to approvals, and instead called for a comprehensive data centre strategy and better coordination between participants in the approvals pipeline. Minutes attached to the report showed members of the Public Accountability and Works Committee voted 6-1 to remove recommendations for a state and national moratorium on data centre approvals "until such time as all social and environmental harms can be fully understood". Committee chair Abigail Boyd, an upper house member from the Greens party who cast the lone vote to keep the recommendations, wrote in the report's foreword that an "AI-fuelled data centre frenzy" was "threatening to consume incomprehensibly large volumes of energy and water to feed their demands". "It is increasingly apparent that governments of all persuasions have been suckered in by an AI-fuelled get rich quick scheme, with data centres suiting the needs of governments short on ideas perfectly," she wrote. "But it's a false economy."

Source: Reuters

FAST

NAPA, California, Nov 4 : The US federal government will lay out all the laws and regulations that apply to domestic AI labs later this month, Pentagon Chief Technology Officer Emil Michael said on Wednesday. Michael, who is vice chair of the government's Super Intelligence Task Force, said the group would publicize the regulatory landscape "in the next week or two." The task force is an intergovernmental agency established by President Donald Trump to establish AI policy. Michael, speaking at a Wall Street Journal technology conference in Napa, California, did not provide additional details. "What we're trying to do is create a framework that makes the American people have confidence that these companies are going to do the right thing," he said. "Or else I think what you get is 535 legislators writing a piece of regulation that could kill the industry."

Source: Reuters
